name: Dental tourism (Turkey, Hungary, Mexico)

angle.text: Appearance-focused people travel to Turkey, Hungary and Mexico to get veneers, crowns and similar cosmetic work at lower prices, with the new smile visible once treatment is done. Researchers document the savings, along with follow-up and liability concerns.

summary: Travelling abroad for cheaper cosmetic dental work, with documented savings and documented follow-up and liability concerns.
note: Literature highlights aftercare, accountability and complication-management issues.
currentQuick:
Dental tourism means travelling to another country for dental treatment, often veneers, crowns or implants. Turkey, Hungary and Mexico are frequently named destinations, with Hungary's Mosonmagyaróvár and Mexico's Los Algodones known for dental clinics.
Researchers attribute it to high home costs, waiting times, cheap travel and the internet linking patients to clinics. The same papers note risks around follow-up care and legal recourse.
How it works: Patients arrange treatment, often through online marketing or agents, and travel for a short stay. Cost savings come from lower prices abroad; Hungarian clinics were reported at a third to half of nearby Vienna prices.
Risks and caveats: Literature describes limited follow-up access, difficulty obtaining remedies for malpractice, variable accreditation, and uncertainty about whether home dentists will treat complications.
deepLead:
Dental tourism is travel abroad for dental care. It is a subset of medical tourism, and Hungary, Turkey and Mexico are among the popular destinations . Researchers identify high local cost, delays in access, inexpensive air travel and the internet as drivers .
Papers on the topic note that it can benefit some patients but brings risks, including limited follow-up and uncertainty about responsibility for complications . Much medical tourism data comes from industry sources and news reports .

name: Floss

angle.text: Flossing is used to clear plaque and food from between teeth, supporting healthy gums and fresher breath for a cleaner-looking smile. The American Dental Association recommends daily use, while systematic reviews rate the evidence for its benefit as low certainty.

summary: String for cleaning between teeth: recommended by dental associations, with systematic reviews rating the evidence low certainty.
note: Guidelines changed in 2015 US dietary guidance omission; ADA continues to recommend daily use.
currentQuick:
Dental floss is thread or tape used to clean between teeth. The American Dental Association recommends flossing once a day, and it is routine in dental advice. It appears in looksmaxxing lists as basic teeth upkeep.
Systematic reviews have judged the evidence that adding floss to brushing improves plaque or gingivitis to be low to very low certainty.
How it works: Floss mechanically disrupts plaque on surfaces a toothbrush misses. Types include waxed or unwaxed nylon or silk, tape, picks, threaders and powered flossers.
Risks and caveats: Misuse can cut gums or cause finger circulation problems if wrapped too tightly, and fibres can catch on dental work.
deepLead:
Dental floss is a thread, usually nylon or silk, used to clean between the teeth. It comes waxed or unwaxed, monofilament or multifilament, with tape, picks, threaders and powered flossers as alternatives . The American Dental Association recommends daily flossing before or after brushing .
Evidence is mixed. A 2011 Cochrane review found some evidence that flossing reduces gingivitis but weak evidence for plaque reduction, and a 2019 Cochrane review of interdental cleaning devices rated the evidence as low to very low certainty . The 2015 US Dietary Guidelines dropped the flossing recommendation, which an August 2016 Associated Press article reported; HHS said it was not questioning efficacy .

name: Interdental brushes

angle.text: Users reach for interdental brushes to clean the gaps and around braces where a toothbrush struggles, aiming for healthy gums and a cleaner smile. Reviews link them to less plaque and gum inflammation than brushing alone.

summary: Tiny brushes for the gaps between teeth; reviews link them to less plaque and gum inflammation than brushing alone.
note: Size must match the gap; evidence concerns gum health, not cosmetics.
currentQuick:
Interdental brushes are small bristled brushes that fit between teeth to clean plaque from spaces a normal toothbrush misses.
Systematic reviews have generally found adding them to toothbrushing is associated with less plaque and gum inflammation, though certainty varies by outcome.
How it works: Bristles or elastomer fins are passed through the gap between teeth to physically disrupt plaque on the side surfaces of teeth and along the gum margin.
Risks and caveats: The research reviewed focuses on efficacy. Brushes sized too large or used forcefully can irritate gums, and sizes are graded by the ISO 16409 standard for that reason.
deepLead:
Interdental brushes are small, bristled brushes, usually on a short handle, designed to pass through the gaps between teeth and around orthodontic hardware to remove plaque from surfaces a regular toothbrush reaches poorly. They are sold over the counter in graded sizes, typically alongside floss, picks and similar devices.
Systematic reviews, including Cochrane reviews, have examined interdental cleaning devices as an addition to toothbrushing for plaque, gum inflammation and tooth decay. Researchers generally report that interdental brushing alongside toothbrushing is associated with lower plaque and gingival inflammation than toothbrushing alone, with the certainty of the evidence described as limited for some outcomes. Interdental brushes are discussed in looksmaxxing circles mainly in the context of gum health and the look of the gum line.

name: Chlorhexidine mouthwash

angle.text: Chlorhexidine rinse is used alongside brushing to cut plaque and gum inflammation, supporting healthier gums and a fresher mouth. It is the best-studied antiplaque rinse, with staining and taste change documented as accompanying effects.

summary: The reference antiplaque rinse; well studied for plaque, but staining and taste change come with it.
note: Tooth staining and altered taste with longer use; labels advise limited duration.
currentQuick:
Chlorhexidine mouthwash is an antiseptic rinse used alongside brushing to cut plaque and mild gum inflammation. It is widely studied and is often the comparator in trials of other mouthwashes.
It is also used in hospital care, for example in oral care for ventilated patients and in cancer-related mouth sores.
How it works: It is a cationic antiseptic that binds to teeth, mucosa and bacterial membranes, giving a lingering antibacterial effect in the mouth.
Risks and caveats: Common effects are brown tooth staining after a month or more, taste disturbance and dry or irritated mouth; allergic reactions are rare. Labels advise limiting use of the mouthwash to about six months. A 2020 study found a week of use shifted the oral microbiome.
deepLead:
Chlorhexidine mouthwash is an antiseptic oral rinse, generally in the 0.05 to 0.2 percent range, used as an adjunct to toothbrushing to reduce dental plaque and gingivitis. Chlorhexidine itself came into medical use in the 1950s and is on the World Health Organization Essential Medicines List.
Researchers describe it as one of the most studied antiplaque agents, and it has also been trialled in hospital settings, such as preventing ventilator-associated pneumonia and treating oral mucositis in cancer patients. Known adverse effects include tooth staining, taste disturbance and, rarely, allergic reactions. Its place in looksmaxxing discussion is mainly as a prescription or pharmacy rinse associated with gum and breath care.

name: Cetylpyridinium chloride mouthwash

angle.text: CPC rinses are the standard drugstore antibacterial mouthwash, used to cut plaque and bad breath for a fresher mouth. Studies show a modest added plaque benefit that is weaker than chlorhexidine, with some staining reported.

summary: The standard drugstore antibacterial rinse; modest added plaque benefit, weaker than chlorhexidine, with some staining.
note: Tooth staining in a small share of users; temporary taste changes reported.
currentQuick:
CPC mouthwash is the common over-the-counter antibacterial rinse, usually at about 0.05 percent. Reviews describe a small added benefit over brushing alone for plaque and gum inflammation.
It also drew research interest during COVID-19 because it breaks down the lipid coat of some viruses.
How it works: CPC is a positively charged quaternary ammonium compound that binds to and disrupts bacterial and viral membranes.
Risks and caveats: Tooth staining is reported in roughly 3 percent of users and taste alteration is usually temporary. The US FDA monograph covers short-term OTC use at 0.025 to 0.1 percent.
deepLead:
Cetylpyridinium chloride (CPC) mouthwash is an over-the-counter antiseptic rinse built around a quaternary ammonium compound that kills bacteria and disrupts the membranes of enveloped viruses. Typical products contain about 0.05 percent CPC and are sold for plaque, gingivitis and bad breath.
Reviews report a small but significant added benefit on plaque and gingivitis when CPC rinses are used with toothbrushing, generally less than chlorhexidine. Tooth staining and temporary taste changes are reported side effects. During the COVID-19 pandemic, CPC rinses were also trialled for reducing SARS-CoV-2 in saliva.

name: Zinc mouthwash (TheraBreath)

angle.text: Zinc rinses such as TheraBreath are used to neutralise the volatile sulfur compounds behind bad breath, for fresher breath up close. Zinc has trial data in other mouth uses, but none specific to this product's effect on breath was found.

summary: A zinc and chlorine dioxide breath rinse; zinc has trial data for mouth sores, but none found for this product on breath.
note: Breath claims for this brand are not tested in the studies found.
currentQuick:
Zinc mouthwashes such as TheraBreath are sold to neutralise the sulphur compounds behind bad breath.
Published zinc studies mostly look at mouth ulcers and mucositis, not breath, and none specific to the brand were found.
How it works: Zinc ions are described as binding volatile sulphur compounds, and chlorine dioxide as oxidising them, which is the basis for the marketing claims.
Risks and caveats: The sources reviewed report no product-specific harms. Zinc in a chlorhexidine rinse is reported to reduce staining.
deepLead:
Zinc-containing mouthwashes, including the TheraBreath line marketed for bad breath, combine zinc ions with other agents such as chlorine dioxide to bind or neutralise the volatile sulphur compounds that cause oral malodour. Wikipedia notes zinc is used with other antiseptics in rinses, and that zinc formulations with chlorhexidine stain less.
Published research on zinc rinses mostly concerns mouth sores and mucositis rather than breath, and no trial specific to the TheraBreath product appears in the literature reviewed. A 2025 dental review looked at cetylpyridinium chloride and zinc rinses together.

name: Alcohol-free mouthwash

angle.text: People choose alcohol-free rinses for regular breath and gum care, often for dry-mouth comfort or to avoid ethanol. How well each performs depends on its active ingredient, such as CPC or essential oils, and the alcohol–oral cancer concern is described as inconclusive.

summary: Mouthwash without ethanol, usually for dry-mouth comfort; effectiveness depends on the active ingredient.
note: Hospital outbreaks traced to contaminated alcohol-free products have been reported.
currentQuick:
Alcohol-free mouthwash is any oral rinse made without ethanol, often chosen by people who find alcohol rinses drying or irritating.
Trials exist for individual formulations with CPC, propolis or essential oils, but the category itself is defined by what it leaves out.
How it works: Antibacterial action comes from the other ingredients, such as CPC, essential oils or plant extracts, rather than from alcohol.
Risks and caveats: Hospital outbreaks of Burkholderia cepacia infection were traced to contaminated alcohol-free mouthwash. Wikipedia describes the evidence linking alcohol-containing rinses to oral cancer as inconclusive.
deepLead:
Alcohol-free mouthwash is a category of oral rinse formulated without ethanol, often with cetylpyridinium chloride, essential oils, herbal extracts or other active ingredients. Wikipedia notes many newer products omit alcohol partly over concern about a possible link to oral cancer, which it describes as inconclusive, and to suit people who avoid alcohol.
Its looksmaxxing relevance is mainly breath and dry-mouth comfort. Trials of alcohol-free rinses include CPC, propolis, chitosan-curcuminoid and essential oil formulations. Hospital outbreaks of Burkholderia cepacia infection traced to contaminated alcohol-free mouthwash have also been published.

name: Essential oil mouthwash (Listerine)

angle.text: Listerine-style rinses are used daily for fresher breath and cleaner teeth and gums. Trials show a modest reduction in plaque and gingivitis, with chlorhexidine still stronger on plaque.

summary: The classic Listerine-style rinse; reduces plaque and gingivitis modestly, with CHX still stronger on plaque.
note: Original versions contain about 22 to 27 percent alcohol; alcohol-free versions exist.
currentQuick:
Essential oil mouthwash, best known as Listerine, combines thymol, menthol, eucalyptol and methyl salicylate. It has been sold since 1879 and was the first US over-the-counter mouthwash.
Systematic reviews find it reduces plaque and gingivitis versus brushing alone, though a commentary reports chlorhexidine is better for plaque.
How it works: The oils are described as disrupting bacterial cell walls and inhibiting enzymes, and as penetrating plaque biofilm.
Risks and caveats: Original versions contain about 22 to 27 percent ethanol, which may cause burning or dryness; alcohol-free versions exist. Wikipedia says the alcohol and oral cancer link is inconclusive.
deepLead:
Essential oil mouthwash is a rinse whose active ingredients are thymol, menthol, eucalyptol and methyl salicylate, best known as Listerine. Listerine was developed in 1879 by St. Louis chemist Joseph Lawrence and named after surgeon Joseph Lister.
A 2011 systematic review compared essential oil rinses with chlorhexidine for plaque and gingival inflammation, and a commentary on it concluded the oil rinses may be equivalent for long-term gingival control while chlorhexidine performs better on plaque. Essential oil rinses are used in many looksmaxxing oral care routines for breath and gum care.

name: Chlorine dioxide rinse

angle.text: Chlorine dioxide rinses are used by people targeting bad breath, on the idea that the oxidizer breaks down the volatile sulfur compounds responsible. A small trial base exists for breath; the mouthwash is a different product from the toxic chlorine-dioxide cure products.

summary: An oxidizing alcohol-free mouthwash aimed at breath odor; a small trial base, and not to be confused with the toxic chlorine-dioxide 'cure' products.
note: Ingesting chlorine dioxide products marketed as cures has caused serious harm; the FDA warns against it.
currentQuick:
A chlorine dioxide rinse is a mouthwash with stabilized chlorine dioxide as the active ingredient, sold to reduce bad breath. Users in breath-focused circles favor it because it is alcohol-free and acts chemically on odor compounds.
An 8-week randomized trial tested it against a placebo rinse in people with intrinsic oral malodor, and Wikipedia cites a meta-analysis reporting benefit for halitosis.
How it works: Chlorine dioxide is an oxidizer. The proposed mechanism is oxidation of volatile sulfur compounds, the odorous molecules produced by oral bacteria.
Risks and caveats: Dilute oral rinsing is accepted in mouthwash use, but concentrated chlorine dioxide is toxic. The FDA warns against ingesting chlorine-dioxide products marketed as cures, which have caused serious injury.
deepLead:
A chlorine dioxide rinse is an alcohol-free mouthwash that contains stabilized chlorine dioxide, an oxidizing agent, as its active ingredient. It is marketed mainly for oral malodor (bad breath), and its proponents say it works by chemically neutralizing the volatile sulfur compounds (VSCs) responsible for much of the odor.
A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial published in 2018 tested an unflavored, non-fluoridated, alcohol-free stabilized chlorine dioxide mouthwash over eight weeks in healthy people with clinically diagnosed intrinsic oral malodor, using it as an adjunct to tooth brushing. Wikipedia notes that dilute chlorine dioxide is an antiseptic ingredient in some mouthwashes and cites a meta-analysis reporting that daily use is effective for halitosis.
Chlorine dioxide is also a toxic industrial chemical, and the US Food and Drug Administration has warned against ingesting chlorine-dioxide products marketed as cures, a different use from supervised dilute oral rinsing.

name: Oral probiotics (BLIS K12)

angle.text: BLIS K12 lozenges are taken by people looking for fresher breath by shifting the mouth's bacterial balance. Human evidence for the breath use is thin.

summary: Probiotic lozenges built around S. salivarius K12, pitched for fresher breath; thin human evidence for that use.
note: Breath-specific trial data is sparse; see the S. salivarius K12 entry.
currentQuick:
Oral probiotics such as BLIS K12 lozenges are meant to seed the mouth with bacteria that compete with harmful ones. Breath-focused users take them hoping to reduce odor-producing species.
The breath-specific evidence is limited, with a few small or registered trials and no large published confirmation.
How it works: The K12 strain produces bacteriocin-like substances that can inhibit other bacteria, including strep throat bacteria.
Risks and caveats: S. salivarius is usually harmless but is a rare opportunistic pathogen in people with very low white blood cell counts.
deepLead:
Oral probiotics are live-bacteria products, typically lozenges, intended to colonize the mouth and throat. BLIS K12 is the best-known example in breath-focused discussion; it contains Streptococcus salivarius K12, a strain that produces bacteriocin-like inhibitory substances (BLIS).
Wikipedia describes lozenges containing S. salivarius being sold to support defence against more virulent streptococci, and notes that some strains are being trialed to prevent oral infections. The published evidence specifically for bad breath is limited, and an article on the strain itself covers the research in more detail.

name: Streptococcus salivarius K12

angle.text: S. salivarius K12 is sold in lozenges and promoted for bad breath and oral and throat health. The breath evidence amounts to one small preliminary study.

summary: A bacteriocin-producing oral probiotic sold in lozenges for bad breath; the breath evidence is one small preliminary study.
note: Breath-specific human data is a 23-person preliminary study; larger trials target other conditions.
currentQuick:
S. salivarius K12 is a naturally occurring mouth bacterium strain sold as a probiotic lozenge, often branded BLIS K12. People interested in breath use it to try to shift oral bacteria away from odor-producing species.
The breath evidence is a small 2006 preliminary study of 23 people. Larger, newer trials have focused on other outcomes such as oral mucositis in radiotherapy.
How it works: The strain makes antimicrobial peptides, salivaricin A2 and B, and lab studies report it dampens some epithelial immune responses and persists in the mouth after dosing.
Risks and caveats: Published safety and tolerance studies, including a randomized double-blind trial, exist. S. salivarius as a species can rarely cause bloodstream infection in people with very low white blood cell counts.
deepLead:
Streptococcus salivarius K12 is a strain of a common oral bacterium sold as an oral probiotic, usually in lozenge form and often under the BLIS K12 name. It is promoted for bad breath (halitosis) and for supporting throat and oral health.
The strain produces bacteriocins, antimicrobial peptides called salivaricin A2 and salivaricin B, encoded on a large transmissible plasmid. Researchers proposed that dosing with such strains could crowd out the bacteria that generate malodor. A small preliminary study of 23 subjects with halitosis, published in 2006, examined K12 lozenges after a chlorhexidine rinse regimen.
Safety assessments of K12, including a randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind tolerance study, have been published. More recent trials have examined other uses, such as oral mucositis during head and neck radiotherapy.

name: Zinc lozenges

angle.text: Zinc lozenges are best known as a cold remedy, and some oral-care users also take them hoping zinc neutralises the sulfur compounds behind bad breath. The cold data is mixed and the breath use is untested.

summary: Cold-remedy lozenges that some breath-focused users take to neutralize sulfur compounds; the cold data is mixed and the breath use is untested.
note: Studied for colds, not breath; taste and mouth irritation are the commonly reported side effects.
currentQuick:
Zinc lozenges are dissolving tablets of a zinc salt, mainly sold for colds. Some people also use them for breath, reasoning that zinc binds smelly sulfur compounds.
Cold trials show mixed results, and no lozenge trial in the sources reviewed tested them for breath.
How it works: For colds, the proposed mechanism is zinc acting locally in the throat, and lab work has examined zinc salts against rhinoviruses. The breath rationale, binding of sulfur compounds, is a proposal without lozenge trials.
Risks and caveats: Trials report bad taste and mouth irritation. Zinc nasal products were linked to loss of smell and drew an FDA warning in 2009, which did not cover oral lozenges.
deepLead:
Zinc lozenges are dissolvable tablets containing a zinc salt, most often zinc gluconate or zinc acetate. They are best known as a common cold remedy, and some people in oral-care circles also use them in the belief that zinc neutralizes the sulfur compounds behind bad breath.
The cold literature is large: randomized trials since 1984 have tested zinc lozenges, with some reporting shorter cold duration and others reporting no benefit, and reviews describe mixed results. No trial in the sources reviewed here tests zinc lozenges for breath or other appearance outcomes; a registered trial comparing probiotic with zinc-chlorhexidine mouthwash for halitosis in orthodontic patients involves a different product.

name: Xylitol gum

angle.text: Xylitol gum is chewed for fresher breath and cleaner teeth, with the sweetener promoted for cutting cavity-causing bacteria and boosting saliva. Trials link it to lower plaque bacteria; benefits beyond plaque are less settled.

summary: Xylitol-sweetened gum that trials link to lower plaque bacteria; benefits beyond plaque are less settled.
note: Highly toxic to dogs; high intake can be laxative.
currentQuick:
Xylitol gum is chewing gum sweetened with a sugar alcohol instead of sugar. Users chew it to cut down plaque bacteria and get more saliva.
Several randomized trials measured mutans streptococci and plaque, and a 2022 review cited by Wikipedia found reduced plaque. Cochrane found the evidence for most xylitol products insufficient.
How it works: Xylitol is thought to suppress growth of pathogenic oral streptococci, and chewing stimulates saliva.
Risks and caveats: High intake can cause gas and diarrhea. Xylitol is toxic to dogs, and the FDA considers it safe as a sweetener for people.
deepLead:
Xylitol gum is chewing gum sweetened with xylitol, a sugar alcohol, rather than sugar. It is promoted for reducing cavity-causing bacteria and plaque and for stimulating saliva.
Trials have measured mutans streptococci in plaque and saliva after xylitol gum, including a dose-response study of 132 participants. A 2022 review cited by Wikipedia found that xylitol chewing gum reduces plaque, while a 2015 Cochrane review found insufficient evidence for most xylitol products other than fluoride toothpaste.

name: Xylitol mints

angle.text: Xylitol mints are used by people who want fresh breath without feeding oral bacteria and who want more saliva. Evidence so far comes from lab models rather than human trials.

summary: Sugar-free mints sweetened with xylitol; only lab-model evidence so far.
note: Toxic to dogs; high intake can be laxative.
currentQuick:
Xylitol mints are breath mints made with xylitol rather than sugar. Users choose them for fresh breath and saliva stimulation without sugar.
The only direct study is a 2017 laboratory simulator, and a 2022 review cited by Wikipedia found xylitol candy did not reduce plaque the way gum did.
How it works: Xylitol is thought to suppress oral streptococci, and sucking a mint stimulates saliva.
Risks and caveats: High intake can cause gas and diarrhea. Xylitol is toxic to dogs.
deepLead:
Xylitol mints are breath mints sweetened with xylitol instead of sugar, used by people who want fresh breath without feeding oral bacteria and who want to stimulate saliva.
Direct evidence is thin. A 2017 laboratory study used a dental simulator to compare commercial xylitol and sucrose mint products on Streptococcus mutans adherence and growth. Wikipedia's xylitol article does not discuss mints specifically, and a 2022 review it cites found that xylitol chewing gum reduces plaque while xylitol candy does not.

name: Sugar-free gum

angle.text: Sugar-free gum is chewed to freshen breath for a while and to boost saliva, which dental researchers describe as protective for teeth. The dental trials concern cavities rather than appearance.

summary: Sugar alcohol gum that boosts saliva and briefly freshens breath; dental trials are about cavities, not looks.
note: Large amounts of sugar alcohols can cause digestive upset.
currentQuick:
Sugar-free gum is chewing gum sweetened with sugar alcohols instead of sugar. People use it to freshen breath and keep the mouth moist.
Dental research supports a role for saliva in protecting teeth, and several trials tested gum for cavities. Evidence for lasting breath or appearance benefits is limited.
How it works: Chewing stimulates saliva, which clears debris and buffers plaque acids.
Risks and caveats: Large amounts of sorbitol or mannitol can cause gas or diarrhoea. Swallowed gum is a concern for young children.
deepLead:
Sugar-free chewing gum is gum sweetened with sugar alcohols such as xylitol, sorbitol, maltitol or isomalt, often with small amounts of intense sweeteners such as aspartame or sucralose. In oral-care and appearance discussions it is used mainly to freshen breath temporarily and to stimulate saliva, which dental researchers describe as protective for teeth.
Clinical research on sugar-free gum has focused on tooth decay rather than looks. A review of clinical caries trials examined whether gum-induced salivary flow helps clear food particles and neutralise plaque acids, and trials have tested gums containing added calcium-phosphate complexes for enamel remineralisation. Wikipedia notes that evidence for gum as a halitosis treatment is not supported by strong data.

name: Breath mints

angle.text: Breath mints are eaten before or after social occasions to get fresh-smelling breath quickly. Dental sources and Wikipedia describe the effect as short-term masking rather than treatment of the cause of odor.

summary: Minty candy that masks breath for a short while without addressing the cause.
note: Masking only; peppermint may aggravate reflux.
currentQuick:
Breath mints are mint-flavoured candies eaten to freshen breath. They are cheap and portable.
Sources describe the effect as short-term masking. Few clinical trials have tested mints specifically.
How it works: Strong mint flavour covers odour, and sugar-free types may stimulate saliva.
Risks and caveats: Generally low risk; peppermint may worsen reflux and some mints contain sweeteners that bother sensitive people.
deepLead:
Breath mints are small mint-flavoured candies eaten to improve breath odour before or after social occasions. Wikipedia describes them as hard, soft or Scotch-style confections flavoured with mint or wintergreen oils. Dental sources and Wikipedia's halitosis article characterise mints and similar products as short-term masking rather than treatment of the cause of odour.
Published clinical work on mints is thin; one study compared oxidising lozenges with breath mints and chewing gum for malodour, and another tested sorbitol-sweetened mints on salivary flow in people with dry mouth.

name: Breath strips

angle.text: Breath strips are dissolving flavour films used for a fast breath refresh before close contact. They borrow fast-dissolving film technology from drug delivery, and no trials on their effect on breath have been published.

summary: Dissolving flavour films for a quick breath refresh; no trials on their effect.
note: Little published evidence specific to breath strips.
currentQuick:
Breath strips are thin films that dissolve on the tongue and release mint flavour.
No clinical studies of their effect on breath were found; the format itself comes from fast-dissolving drug films.
How it works: The film dissolves quickly and the flavour masks odour for a short time.
Risks and caveats: No specific risks are documented in the sources reviewed.
deepLead:
Breath strips are thin, flavoured films that dissolve on the tongue within moments and are sold to freshen breath. They use fast-dissolving film technology, which was developed as an oral delivery format for drugs and is described in pharmaceutical reviews as a film that dissolves in under a minute.
No clinical trials of breath strips for breath odour were found; sources describe the product format rather than its effectiveness.

name: Parsley and mint chewing

angle.text: Chewing fresh parsley or mint is a folk habit for freshening breath, especially after garlic- or onion-heavy meals. Parsley is credited in cooking with neutralising garlic odors, but the breath effect is untested in trials.

summary: Folk habit of chewing fresh herbs for fresh breath; untested in trials.
note: No studies; effect, if any, is brief.
currentQuick:
Some people chew fresh parsley or mint after meals to freshen breath.
No clinical studies were found, and sources describe such remedies as at most short-term masking.
How it works: Fresh herb flavour and chewing-induced saliva may cover odour briefly.
Risks and caveats: Low in food amounts; peppermint can aggravate reflux and parsley seeds are not recommended in pregnancy.
deepLead:
Chewing fresh parsley or mint leaves is a folk method for freshening breath, often after garlic- or onion-heavy meals. Parsley is widely used as a garnish and is described on Wikipedia as being credited in cooking with neutralising garlic odours.
Wikipedia's halitosis article reports that dietary approaches lack strong evidence and describes mints and similar remedies as short-term masking. No clinical study of chewing parsley or mint leaves for breath was found.

name: Chlorophyll tablets

angle.text: Chlorophyll tablets are marketed as internal deodorants, and users take them hoping to reduce breath and body odor. The one controlled odor trial found no difference from placebo.

summary: Chlorophyllin pills sold as internal deodorants; the one controlled odour trial found no difference from placebo.
note: Odour claims described as unsubstantiated.
currentQuick:
Chlorophyll tablets are supplements sold to reduce breath and body odour from the inside.
A small controlled trial in colostomy patients found no difference from placebo, and the odour claims are described as unsubstantiated.
How it works: Chlorophyllin is claimed to bind odour compounds; this is not established for appearance use.
Risks and caveats: The sources reviewed give no adverse-effect profile. It is a permitted food colouring.
deepLead:
Chlorophyll tablets contain chlorophyll or, more often, chlorophyllin, a water-soluble semi-synthetic salt of chlorophyll used as a food colouring (E140 and E141). They are marketed as internal deodorants for breath, body, urine and faecal odour.
Wikipedia calls these deodorant claims unsubstantiated. A randomised, double-blind crossover study in 28 colostomy patients found no difference from placebo in subjective odour. Research on chlorophyllin now focuses on radiation-related conditions in registered trials.

name: Salt water rinse

angle.text: Warm salt water rinses are a low-cost home habit for soothing sore gums and keeping the mouth clean. Saline is described as a mechanical cleanser with antiseptic action, and one school trial compared it with chlorhexidine.

summary: Warm salt-and-water home rinse used to soothe gums; compared with chlorhexidine in one school trial.
note: After extractions, guidance says to hold the rinse passively at first.
currentQuick:
A salt water rinse is a homemade mouthwash used for sore gums and general cleaning.
Saline is described as mildly antiseptic, and one school trial compared it with chlorhexidine.
How it works: Salt solution mechanically cleans and is hypertonic to bacteria.
Risks and caveats: Low; after dental extractions, guidance advises gentle holding rather than vigorous swishing.
deepLead:
A salt water rinse is a rinse of warm water with dissolved salt, used as a low-cost mouthwash for gum soreness and mouth hygiene. Wikipedia describes saline as a mechanical cleanser with antiseptic action because it is hypertonic to bacteria.
A school-based randomised trial compared salt water with chlorhexidine for effects on dental plaque and oral microbes. Wikipedia's mouthwash article does not discuss salt water for gingivitis specifically or for bad breath.
